transcript.text: Good morning, Maya and Nadia. As Patent Counsel, I have a status update that bears directly on this license. After the draft was circulated, I pulled the latest patent-maintenance records, and there are two important findings the group needs to be aware of before any approval decision. First, enforceable portfolio coverage for this license currently exists only in the United States and Germany — not worldwide as the proposed license suggests. Second, the maintenance fee for US Patent 11-482901 is due in just 9 days, and we need to ensure that fee is paid to preserve that coverage. I have not yet added these updated records to the patent schedule, which is why I'm flagging them now. Nadia, I'm also very interested to hear about the discrepancy you've identified, as it may compound the concerns I'm raising.

The approved business term sheet — which I confirmed directly with HelioGrid's commercial sponsor — permits exclusivity only for grid-scale battery storage applications, not the broader scope suggested in the proposed draft. It sets the royalty at exactly 6% of net sales, not the 5% that appears in HelioGrid's proposed license. And it prohibits sublicensing entirely, which directly conflicts with the unrestricted sublicensing rights in the proposed draft. I should also note that HelioGrid's commercial sponsor indicated they will not sign on the broader draft terms. transcript.text: Thank you, Nadia. This is extremely concerning. The discrepancies you've identified are substantial and compound the patent-coverage issues I raised. Let me summarize what we're now looking at: First, on territorial scope, the proposed draft grants a worldwide exclusive license, but enforceable patent coverage exists only in the United States and Germany. We'd be granting exclusivity in jurisdictions where we have no enforceable rights to back it up. Second, the royalty rate in the draft is 5%, but the approved term sheet specifies 6%. Third, the draft permits unrestricted sublicensing, but the term sheet prohibits sublicensing entirely. And fourth, the scope of exclusivity in the draft appears broader than the grid-scale battery storage applications limitation in the term sheet. Any one of these discrepancies would be enough to warrant holding approval. Taken together, it's clear this draft cannot be approved as written. I'd recommend we direct HelioGrid to revise the draft to align with the confirmed term sheet terms, and in parallel, I'll get the maintenance fee for US Patent 11-482901 processed immediately so we don't lose that coverage. Maya, I'd defer to you on how you'd like to proceed with the approval decision given these findings.
